cards.explanation: The answer is Jesus our Lord. Paul, the apostle who wrote this letter, asks, "Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?" He puts it between "Am I not an apostle?" and "Are you yourselves not my workmanship in the Lord?" That's four questions in a row, friends. I can barely get through a recipe without losing my place.

The answer is that the Corinthians themselves are the seal. Paul says, "For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord." On my cookie boxes, the seal is what tells you it's the real thing. Paul says the Corinthians are that mark for his apostleship. Just before this he calls them "…my workmanship in the Lord?" so the proof is the people his work reached.

The answer is a believing wife. Paul asks, "Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas?" Cephas is Peter (John 1:42). So Paul is pointing at the other apostles and asking what's fair for himself and Barnabas. Notice he calls her a believing wife, so the text says she shares the faith.

The answer is True. Paul asks, "Or are Barnabas and I the only apostles who must work for a living?" Barnabas is the man Paul names beside himself. He asks it as a question, and he's pointing at the other apostles. He's asking if the two of them got stuck with the day jobs.

The point of all three questions is that a worker shares in what he works for. Paul asks about a soldier who doesn't pay his own way, a vineyard planter who eats its fruit and a shepherd who drinks the flock's milk. In each case the worker is expected to get something from the work. Three questions and one point, friends.

The answer is True. Paul points to the Law of Moses, and the line is: "Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10). So Paul isn't just giving his own opinion. He goes straight to the Law to back up what he's saying.

The word is harvest. Paul says, "…when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they should also expect to share in the harvest." He has just asked if God is really concerned about oxen, and he says this was written for us. So the point isn't about oxen at all. People who do the hard work of spreading the gospel can expect to be supported by the people they serve, and that's why Paul goes on to say, "If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?" (1 Corinthians 9:11).

The word is material. Paul asks, "If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much for us to reap a material harvest from you?" Spiritual seed on one side, a material harvest on the other. He ties it right back to the farm talk about the plowman and the thresher.

The answer is False. Paul says, "But we did not exercise this right." He just argued that he has it all the more, and then he says he never used it. Having a right and choosing not to use it are two different things, and that's the twist in the verse. Instead, he says, "…we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ."

The answer is so he wouldn't hinder the gospel of Christ. Paul says, "…we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ." Anything, friends. That's not a small word, and he picked it on purpose. He has the right and he puts it down, because the gospel matters more to him.

The answer is those who preach the gospel. Paul says, "…the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel." He starts with temple workers eating of the temple's food, then says the Lord set up the same kind of thing for gospel preachers. It's a pattern, friends. The workers get their living from the work they do.

The answer is False. Paul says it plainly: "And I am not writing this to suggest that something be done for me." He built the whole case, and he's not collecting on it. It's like spending all morning making your case to the boss for a raise and then saying you're not asking for one.

The word is obligated. Paul says, "…I have no reason to boast, because I am obligated to preach." Then he adds, "Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!" So he doesn't treat preaching as something to brag about. He treats it as something he has to do.

The answer is offering the gospel free of charge. Paul says his reward is "That in preaching the gospel I may offer it free of charge, and so not use up my rights in preaching it." He has the rights, and he doesn't spend them. The reward he names is giving it away free.

The answer is True. Paul says, "Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible." It sounds backward, and it is. Free, and then a slave to everyone. He gives the reason too, which is to win as many as possible.

The answer is the law of Christ. Paul says he's "…not outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ…" He becomes like one without the law for those without it, yet he doesn't leave God's law behind. He says he's under the law of Christ.

The word is save. Paul says, "I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some." That's the reason behind all the becoming he just described. Whether it's the Jews, those under the law, those without it or the weak, the aim stays the same: that he might save some.

The answer is to share in its blessings. Paul says, "I do all this for the sake of the gospel, so that I may share in its blessings." Everything he just described, becoming all things to all people, is for the gospel. And he says he hopes to share in its blessings himself.
The answer is False. Paul says, "Run in such a way as to take the prize." Only one receives it, and he still says to run. He doesn't tell them to sit down, he tells them to run like they mean it.

The answer is that it will never perish. Paul says the athletes "…do it for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable." Perishable means it can wear out and fade, and imperishable means it never will. So the athletes chase a prize that doesn't last, while ours does.

The answer is beating the air. Paul says, "…I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air." Beating the air is a picture of swinging with nothing there to hit. He sets it right beside running aimlessly, so both lines are about effort with no aim.

The word is body. Paul says, "No, I discipline my body and make it my slave…" He starts with the race and the fight, then brings it back to himself. The training he talks about starts with his own body.

The answer is so he won't be disqualified himself. Paul says it's "…so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified." He's been telling others, and he says he doesn't want to be disqualified himself. It's a humble note to end on, friends.
